definition: Figurative means expressing meaning through imagery rather than literal statement.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word figurative. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know figurative should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Nobody at the seed store believed the tomatoes truly drink sunshine, and the clerk's figurative pitch still sold out the flat by noon.
Vivid is milder than figurative — vivid wording paints sharply but can stay perfectly literal; a vivid fact is still a fact.
Fantastical goes further than figurative: figurative language borrows an image while meaning something real, but the fantastical leaves reality behind altogether.

Metaphorical names one specific move: speaking through one thing to mean another, as when a deadline 'looms' or a rumor 'spreads like wildfire.' Figurative is the umbrella over that move and its cousins — simile, hyperbole, personification. Every metaphorical phrase is figurative; not every figurative phrase is a metaphor.

Symbolic points at objects and images set up to stand for something beyond themselves — a dove for peace, a broken clock for lost time. Figurative describes wording instead: language that trades literal statement for imagery. A symbol sits in the scene; figurative language lives in the phrasing.

When the news anchor says the river 'shrugged off' the new levee, she speaks in images: rivers have no shoulders, but the borrowed shrug captures what the footage showed — water moving past the barrier as if it were not there.
That is figurative speech at work.
Figurative is the umbrella term for meaning carried by imagery instead of literal statement — and it is not a polite word for false.
The water really did move past; only the shrug was borrowed.
If every element of a whole work carries a second meaning, you have moved past figurative language into allegory.
Figurative is the wide, workhorse label: any wording that trades literal statement for imagery.
Reach for it when you need the umbrella; reach for allegory when a whole work sustains the second meaning, and for allusion when the figure points quietly at another work.

The postcards from Aunt Bea arrived every June, and for years Tomas read them like weather reports.
'This town is an oven,' one said, and he pictured bakery racks; 'the mosquitoes are the size of sparrows,' said another, and he worried for the birds.
His sister finally set him straight on the porch: Aunt Bea writes in figurative language, meaning through pictures, and not one of her sentences is a lie so much as a painting.
The town was hot, the mosquitoes were thick; the oven and the sparrows were just her way of making him feel it.
That June, Tomas wrote back in kind, reporting that his summer reading list had 'swallowed the living room.'
